clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant, slowly progressive and largely pure cerebellar ataxia caused by variants, often in-frame deletions or missense changes, in SPTBN2, which encodes beta-III spectrin
Historically termed 'Lincoln ataxia' after a large American kindred descended from the paternal grandparents of Abraham Lincoln
Onset ranges from childhood to mid-adulthood, progression is slow and life expectancy is usually near-normal
Clinical features are gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and eye-movement abnormalities including downbeat and gaze-evoked nystagmus, with facial myokymia in some patients
Beta-III spectrin anchors the glutamate transporter EAAT4 and receptors at the Purkinje cell membrane, so its dysfunction impairs glutamate handling
Diagnosis is by gene sequencing, since repeat-expansion assays are normal
Brain MRI typically shows marked and relatively isolated cerebellar atrophy
Biallelic SPTBN2 variants cause a distinct severe infantile-onset recessive ataxia, in contrast to the dominant SCA5
reference.pathophysiology: SCA5 is caused by dominant variants in SPTBN2, which encodes beta-III spectrin, a cytoskeletal protein enriched in Purkinje cells that stabilises membrane proteins, including the glutamate transporter EAAT4, and helps organise the neuronal membrane skeleton. Mutant spectrin mislocalises or fails to anchor these proteins, so glutamate clearance and Purkinje cell membrane integrity are impaired. The resulting progressive Purkinje cell dysfunction and degeneration underlie the largely pure cerebellar ataxia and the associated eye-movement abnormalities.
additionalDifferentials: Other pure autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias (SCA6, SCA14, SCA28)
Ataxias with prominent downbeat nystagmus, such as episodic ataxia type 2 and FGF14-related ataxia
Severe infantile recessive SPTBN2 ataxia in young children
additionalInvestigations: SPTBN2 sequencing within an ataxia gene panel or exome
Brain MRI to document the marked, relatively isolated cerebellar atrophy
Testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs to exclude commoner causes
Screening for acquired ataxia (thyroid function, vitamins B12 and E, coeliac serology)
Detailed family history to establish autosomal dominant transmission
Consideration of recessive SPTBN2 disease in infantile presentations
redFlags: Rapid progression or an atypical course suggesting an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
A structural lesion at the craniocervical junction as an alternative cause of downbeat nystagmus
A severe infantile presentation suggesting recessive SPTBN2 disease
Dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallow assessment
reference.prognosis: SCA5 is slowly progressive over decades, with ambulation often preserved for prolonged periods and a near-normal lifespan typical; disability is driven by cumulative cerebellar dysfunction, and prognosis is generally more favourable than in many other spinocerebellar ataxias.
pitfalls: Expecting a repeat expansion and missing the point mutation or in-frame deletion when common panels are negative
Confusing dominant SCA5 with the distinct severe infantile recessive SPTBN2 disorder
Attributing downbeat nystagmus to a structural lesion only, without considering a genetic ataxia
Not proceeding to sequencing after negative repeat panels
Failing to provide genetic counselling regarding dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is symptomatic and supportive, centred on maintaining function and preventing falls
Physiotherapy with balance and gait rehabilitation, and occupational therapy for mobility aids and home adaptation
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria, with swallow assessment and dietary modification as dysphagia develops
Symptomatic treatment of downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus and oscillopsia with aminopyridine-class agents, and of troublesome facial myokymia
Periodic neurological review to monitor progression, falls risk and nutritional and swallowing status
Genetic counselling with predictive and cascade testing for at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
Referral to specialist ataxia multidisciplinary services and patient support organisations
